# South Manmarch · Book II, pp. 350–355
# Generated by the extractor — fix the extractor, not this file.
PAGE	350
P	If you descend from the <b>Steplands</b> (page 372) to the southeast, you'll find yourself on a rolling prairie. The ground slopes gently down toward the east, to the banks of the <b>Dread River</b> (page 86).
P	Travelers and merchants aplenty cross these plains. They come north, from <b>Lygos</b> <b>and the civilized south</b> (page 256), heading north to the <b>Highway</b> (page 270) and from there to <b>Marshedge</b> (page 274).
P	Or they head the other way, bearing herbs and textiles, metals and gems, back to the southern cities. Or they come from beyond the Highway, from the <b>North Manmarch</b> (page 282), to hunt or trade or raid.
P	But for all those who pass through the South Manmarch, few call it home. Sure, the <b>Hillfolk</b> (page 228) graze their herds here in the warmer months. And some new settlement is always popping up. But the land is dotted with burnt-out homesteads and ruined forts: a mute testament to those who have tried to settle here before. Tried, and failed.

PAGE	351
H2	A long-disputed land
HR
P	Before the <b>Cataclysm</b> (page 412) the Dread River formed the eastern border of <b>Stone</b> <b>Lord</b> (page 382) territory. After the Stone Lords fell, the <b>Barrow Builders</b> (page 34) fought each other back and forth across this expanse, grinding themselves down, like shards of shale abraded to dust over time.
P	Now, the South Manmarch is the border between the civilized south and the hinterlands of the World's End. It's a lawless place, full of dangerous beasts and even more dangerous people. Nomadic Hillfolk claim much of the region, and <b>bandits</b> (page 355) are a constant threat.
P	And yet, the lure of the prairie is great.
P	Every year or so, someone tries to carve out a piece of for themselves. A new settlement might be:
B	A family from Marshedge or the North Manmarch, starting their own farm
B	An ambitious Lygosi merchant, investing in a new trading post or caravansary
B	Some would-be chief or warlord from the <b>Manmarchers</b> (page 282), building a new hamlet or hillfort
B	The <b>conquering armies</b> of the South (page 262), establishing a foothold Such settlements rarely last. They fall prey to natural disaster or roving beasts, to rivals or bandits, or to the certain wrath of the Hillfolk who claim these lands as theirs.
P	Or perhaps, if you believe the stories, there's something darker afoot. Perhaps these lands really are haunted. Haunted by the numerous souls who've died here. Or by foul things, slithering out of the Dread River. Perhaps the land is cursed, and no settlement can ever survive. Perhaps.
H2	The Flintwash
P	Draining out of the Steplands and into the Dread River, this watercourse draws thickets, copses of cottonwood, wildlife, and wanderers to its gentle banks. The Hillfolk call it <i>Maengwalc</i> in their own tongue—"Flintwash," after the stony plateau from which its headwaters spring.
P	Hundreds of rills and brooks feed the Flintwash, and in its lower reaches, it's quite broad and difficult to cross. Yet ways do exist. How might a traveler get from one side to the other? Ask a PC who would know, but perhaps there is…
E	an old bridge from the time of the <b>Makers</b> (page 264);
E	a newer bridge, built at great expense by some southern merchant or noble;
E	a shallow ford; wide, rocky and usually safe;
E	a ferry, run by enterprising souls;
E	some combination of the above; or
E	something else entirely.

H2	Questions
HR
Q	Who did you know who tried to settle in the South Manmarch? What fate befell them?
Q	What bandit crew is currently the most feared? Who leads them, and what makes them so dangerous?
Q	At what landmark do merchant caravans typically encamp? Why do they stop there?
Q	What landmark does everyone who travels these lands know to avoid? Why?
H2	Hooks
HR
B	Someone has seized the Flintwash crossing, and is charging exorbitant tolls
B	An ambitious chief from the North Manmarch is sending settlers south of the Highway
B	The PCs eagerly await a caravan, but it gets waylaid by bandits
B	A ruin in the region becomes a place of pilgrimage, drawing the faithful of Helior/Aratis from all over

H3	Hazards
B	Baking sun, no shade for miles
B	Nasty turn in the weather: lashing wind, bitter cold, blistering heat, sleet/ hail/rain/snow; lightning
B	Flash flooding in valleys/on slopes
B	Lack of shelter, water, or wood for a long-burning fire (try dried aurochs dung, if you can find it)
B	Hidden holes/burrows, twisting an ankle or worse

H3	Horned drake
P	<i>Solitary</i>, <i>huge</i>, <i>hardy</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 24; <b>Armor</b> 3 (stony hide)
P	<b>Damage</b> trampling charge d10+5 (<i>hand</i>, <i>area</i>, <i>forceful</i>) or horn gore d10+5 (<i>close</i>, <i>forceful</i>, <i>messy</i>, 1 piercing)
P	<b>Instinct</b> to protect their young
P	• Issue a honking call
P	• Stand its ground, still as a rock
P	• Lurch suddenly into a charge
P	• Absorb raw elemental power (regaining 1d8 HP)
P	The behemoth of the southern grasslands is striking for its great size, the quartz-like plates of its segmented hide, and its fearsome horns. The horns vary greatly from beast to beast, ranging from a single spike on its snout or forehead to a rack of five or six curved points edging the flanges of its massive skull. An intimidating beast, even at rest.
P	To the Hillfolk, the downing of a <i>d'lkornek</i> ("thorn-dragon") is a hero's feat, to be followed by a week of harvest and celebration at the kill site.
P	<b>Something interesting</b>: Some scholars hold that the Stone Lords imbued horned drakes with elemental qualities. Specimens of their hide are commonly mistaken for dolostone or some other mineral, and Hillfolk prize their horns (Value 3).
P	<b>Something useful:</b> The horns of a <i>d'lkornek</i> act like <b>power-crystals</b> (page 389), but larger and with great capacity.
P	They are extremely dangerous to harvest; a wise butcher slowly bleeds away their energy over the course of days.
P	Adult horned drakes might be accompanied
P	by their young (<i>group</i>, <i>large</i>, <i>hardy</i>; <b>HP</b> 14;
P	<b>Damage</b> d8+3; <b>Instinct</b> to get curious, to play fight), whom they aggressively defend.

H3	Bandit
P	<i>Horde</i>, <i>stealthy</i>, <i>cautious</i>, <i>devious</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 3; <b>Armor</b> up to 2 (hides, shields)
P	<b>Damage</b> spear d6 (<i>close</i>, <i>thrown</i>) or sling d6 (<i>near</i>, <i>awkward</i>, <i>reload</i>)
P	<b>Instinct</b> to survive at the expense of others
P	• Block passage, issue a blunt demand
P	• Ambush under cover of darkness
P	• Ransom the best, kill the rest
P	The <b>Makers' Roads</b> (page 270) limit banditry throughout most the World's End.
P	Not so in the South Manmarch. Here, merchants travel without the safety of warded pavestones. And those merchants draw bandits like dung draws flies. They're motley crews, these bandits. Rogues from Marshedge. Deserters from the armies of North and South. Exiled Hillfolk. Scoundrels. Miscreants. Anyone who's willing to get their hands red, really.

P	<i>Group</i>, <i>leader</i>, <i>stealthy</i>, <i>cautious</i>, <i>devious</i>, <i>organized</i>
P	<b>HP</b> 8; <b>Armor</b> 3 (hides, shield, skill)
P	<b>Damage</b> spear d8 (<i>close</i>, <i>thrown</i>, 1 piercing) or bow d8 (<i>near</i>)
P	<b>Instinct</b> to live their best life beyond the reach of the law
P	• Exude a brutal charisma
P	• Demonstrate great skill at arms
P	• Brook no disagreement
P	Every group demands a boss; the exiled and forsaken moreso. What makes this leader stand apart? (pick 2 or 3)
B	Infamy, from deeds real or fabricated
B	Fearlessness, borne of a veteran's confidence or amateur's stupidity
B	Fragile alliance with a Hillfolk band
B	A <b>spirit-of-the-wild</b> familiar (page 356)
